# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declare Stage

When I see my three crates, I calculate their sum immediately.

When deciding what to declare, I declare my true total value. This avoids the -40 penalty from being flagged and lets me score the full value of my hold minus duty.

When my heaviest crate is worth less than 40, I declare my true total without worry—the spot check won't flag me.

When I'm behind in standings late in the game, I don't increase my declaration beyond what's safe just to catch up. The marginal points from aggressive declaring don't compensate for the risk of the -40 flag penalty.

## Route Stage

When I declare my true value and my heaviest crate is clearly below my declaration, I take the main route. The main route gives me all three crates minus a 30% duty, which is better than losing my smallest crate to the night route's 15% duty.

I take the night route only when I have low-value crates and need to minimize the duty I pay, accepting the loss of my smallest crate as a trade-off.

## General Strategy

I play conservatively and honestly. Declaring true value is safer than bluffing because the harbormaster's spot check is mechanical and will catch understated values.

I do not try to outguess other players' declarations. I focus on my own holds and route choices.

When I'm ahead, I maintain my lead with consistent, safe play. When I'm behind, I don't take unnecessary risks with inflated declarations—steady scoring across remaining rounds is more reliable than one aggressive round.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When I declare, I will calculate my true hold total and compare the expected scores from main versus night routes before committing.

When my hold total is moderate (roughly 60-70 points), I will declare truthfully or very close to it, since the risk of a flag is low and the score difference between routes is modest.

When I have a high-value hold (above 75), I will consider declaring slightly below my true total to reduce duty burden while staying safe from flags, since my heaviest crate will likely be well below my declaration.

I will stop defaulting to declaring my true total. I will actively calculate: (hold value - duty for main) versus (hold value - smallest crate - duty for night) and choose the declaration that supports whichever route scores higher.

When choosing a declaration, I will look at what others declared in recent rounds. If the table is declaring in the 70-76 range consistently, I should match that range rather than declaring conservatively low.

## Route Strategy

When I declared a moderate value (60-75 range), the main route was safer and more predictable. I should take main.

When I declared higher (above 75), I should reconsider. I may have been leaving points on the table by not taking night route when my duty was high. Before committing to main, I will calculate whether night's confiscation of my smallest crate actually saves me more in duty than it costs me.

I will not default to main route reflexively. I will calculate both routes' net scores every single time and choose accordingly.

## Position and Competition

I notice I trailed Mirren by about 19 points in the final round. I was too conservative throughout. Declaring higher earlier and taking night route when it beat main would have closed that gap.

I should not let a "safe" mentality keep me in second place repeatedly. When I am behind, I need to declare more aggressively and calculate which route actually maximizes my round score, not which feels safer.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

**On Declaration:**

When I see my three crates, I will add their values and declare that total or very close to it. Honesty is my baseline; it keeps me safe from the spot check penalty that costs 40 points and recalculates duty at the higher rate.

I will always declare at least as much as my heaviest crate to avoid triggering the flag. This is non-negotiable.

When I'm unsure whether to declare exactly my true total or slightly higher, I'll declare my true total. The duty savings from understatement don't justify the downside risk.

**On Route Selection:**

When I have a moderate declaration (in the range of what others are declaring), I will take the main route. The main route gives me floor(0.30 × declared value) duty and I keep all my crates.

I will only take the night route if:
- My declared value is genuinely low (suggesting a weak hand where losing my smallest crate isn't a major sacrifice), OR
- I'm confident my smallest crate is close enough in value to my others that the duty savings outweigh the loss.

In practice, I took main route every time this episode, and it worked consistently. This suggests that in a four-player game where declarations cluster in the 65–78 range, main route is the safer play for moderate hands.

**On Competitive Positioning:**

I will not let my current position in the standings distract me from sound individual-round decisions. Trying to "close a gap" by declaring aggressively in round 6 when my hand (6, 23, 34) was genuinely worth 63 points was a mistake—I declared 78, which I then had to defend on the spot check. This overcomplicated my final round unnecessarily.

Each round stands alone. Maximize this round's score; trust that consistency will handle the tournament.

**On End-Game Thinking:**

In the final round, I don't need a special strategy. I apply the same honest declaration and safe route logic. I finished second; I should have finished first or stayed first. The difference was likely earlier rounds where I played too conservatively given my hands, not final-round aggression.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When you see your three crates, sum their values immediately. Always declare at least the value of your heaviest crate—this is non-negotiable to avoid the -40 penalty flag.

Beyond the safety floor, declare your true total value or slightly above it. The math consistently favors honesty: the duty penalty is manageable when you keep all your crates on the main route, and lying risks catastrophic -40 swings that wreck your score.

When you're trailing in points with rounds remaining, resist the urge to declare far above your hand's value hoping to bluff. Look at what others have declared in recent rounds—your declarations should stay within the range established by the table (typically 65-78 in a four-player game). Declarations that deviate wildly upward invite suspicion and won't improve your final score if you get caught.

## Route Selection

Always take the main route. You ended strong because you chose main every single time. The night route's math looks tempting—lower duty—but losing your smallest crate is a hidden tax that compounds. The main route's higher duty (0.30 vs 0.15) is more than offset by keeping all three crates.

Do not chase variance in the final rounds. A safe, predictable main route score is worth more than gambling on night route luck when you're close to winning.

## Positional Thinking

Track the leaderboard after each round, but do not let it drive you to reckless declarations. Your job is to maximize your own score per round, not to beat specific players. Steady, honest play from behind will close gaps better than desperate overbidding.

In the final round especially, when you're behind: do not overreach. A solid, safe score on main route is better than a speculative high declaration that risks a flag and -40.

HARBOR CUSTOMS -- 4 players, 6 rounds.
You are Vance, among Mirren, Vance, Odalie and Krek.

Each round the harbor deals every seat a private hold of exactly 3 crates, each worth 5-40 points. You see your own crate values; everyone else sees only that you carry 3 crates.

Stage 1 (declare): you write one number on the manifest -- the total value of the crates in your hold. Legal range 0-120.

Stage 2 (route): choose how you enter port.
  main  -- duty = floor(0.30 x your declared value). You keep all 3 crates.
  night -- duty = floor(0.15 x your declared value), but the harbor
           confiscates your SMALLEST crate (its value is lost to you).

Then the harbormaster works the quay. His spot check is the standing one: a dockhand lifts the top crate off each hold -- always the heaviest crate -- puts it on the scale, and the referee flags any manifest whose declared value falls below that crate's value. A flagged seat pays -40 points and its duty is recomputed at 0.30 x the true total value of its hold, whatever route it took.

Each round: score = value of crates you still hold - duty - penalty.

POINTS: Mirren 0, Vance 0, Odalie 0, Krek 0
Reply with [declare: n], an integer from 0 to 120.

Reply with the bracketed token only. One short line of reasoning before it is fine.
turns.content:
My crates total 6 + 27 + 31 = 64 points. My heaviest crate is 31, which is well below 40, so declaring my true value of 64 is safe—the spot check won't flag me. I'll declare honestly and take the main route to keep all three crates.

[declare: 64]
